item.title: Growing Children by Stepping Back
item.description:
Parenting

Growing Children by Stepping Back

What "Toy Story 5" teaches us about free play and parenting.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Free play builds resilience, creativity, and emotional regulation.
  • Parents can foster growth by managing their anxiety, not their child.
  • Technology should complement—not replace—imaginative, social play.
  • Children grow by solving problems, not having every problem solved.

Watching Toy Story 5 with my grandchildren reminded me that some of the most important conversations about child development begin where imagination flourishes. Beneath the humor and adventure lies a thoughtful exploration of one of the defining questions of contemporary childhood: What happens when imaginative, child-led play gradually gives way to increasingly screen-based experiences?

Source: Silvana Carlos/Unsplash

As a family therapist, I find myself asking a slightly different question. Not simply what do children need, but what helps parents create the emotional conditions in which children can flourish? From a Bowen family systems perspective, healthy development is less about adults carefully managing children and more about gradually raising young people who can think for themselves while remaining deeply connected to others. Free play provides one of the richest settings for this kind of growth in childhood.

Why Imaginative Play Still Matters

Developmental psychology has long recognised that imaginative play nurtures creativity, emotional regulation, empathy, flexible thinking, and problem-solving. When children organise games, negotiate rules, work through disagreements, and recover from mistakes, they strengthen capacities that no adult can simply teach through instruction.

Bowen family systems theory reminds us that resilience grows through experience (a relational process) rather than through parenting techniques. As children navigate the ordinary ups and downs of play, they gradually learn to regulate themselves rather than relying on adults to manage every situation. The enduring appeal of the Toy Story films lies in understanding that toys become meaningful because children transform them into stories, friendships, and shared worlds.

Screens Aren't the Solo Villain

One of the film's strengths is its refusal to make technology the villain. Digital devices are now woven into all our lives. The developmental challenge is to ensure that technology complements rather than replaces opportunities for imaginative, embodied, and relational play. The question is not whether screens belong in childhood, but what experiences they may be displacing.

What's Disappearing From Childhood?

Historians Peter Stearns and Steven Mintz argue that perhaps the most revolutionary change in childhood since the Second World War has been the transformation of children's play. They conclude that "the transformation of play was one of the most striking features of the larger shift in American culture" (Stearns & Mintz, 2025).

In The Parenting Paradox, I wrote: "There's an alternative narrative to Haidt's argument, presented by Professor Peter Gray, a research professor at Boston College, who proposes that the loss of free play may have more to do with the decline in mental health than social media."

Rather than asking only what screens are doing to children, perhaps we should also ask what has quietly disappeared from childhood itself. As parents and educators become increasingly responsible for organizing children's lives, opportunities to develop confidence in their own thinking, judgment, and problem-solving can quietly diminish.

Play Reveals the Whole Child

In The Parenting Paradox, I wrote in one of the many parent examples:

"Balanced Love Is Connecting to the Whole Child... Dad Jason began noticing how his three kids liked to play—how their imaginations worked, what activities they loved to repeat, and which stories captured their interest. From these observations, he expanded his repertoire as a father, connecting with each child through a genuine interest in their unique personalities."

Watching children play tells us far more than what they enjoy. It reveals how they approach challenges, relationships, frustration, cooperation, and creativity. Parents often ask me how to connect more deeply with their children. One answer is surprisingly simple: becoming fascinated with their play. Curiosity reduces parental anxiety and fosters a stronger connection than worry and monitoring.

This reflects a central idea running through The Parenting Paradox: Children's development is deeply influenced by the emotional climate their parents contribute to. The parents' own growth is one of the greatest gifts they can offer a child. Rather than asking, "How do I change my child?" the more transformative question becomes, "How do I become the kind of parent who contributes to the conditions for my child to flourish?"

Creating More Space for Play

I often point to the Let Grow movement as a practical example of encouraging children's independence through free play and age-appropriate autonomy. Adults remain available for safety while deliberately resisting the urge to organize every interaction.

For many parents, this is the hardest part. Standing back can feel uncomfortable. Growing yourself up means learning to notice and manage your own anxiety rather than automatically managing your child's experience. When parents become less reactive, more curious, and better able to tolerate uncertainty, children gain opportunities to think, negotiate, recover, and discover their own competence. That is differentiation-based parenting in action.

The Takeaway

Toy Story 5 reminds us that technology belongs in today's world, but it cannot (and must not) replace imagination, friendship, independence, and free play.

The film also offers a gentle challenge for parents. Children's healthy development depends not only on what we provide, but also on what we can refrain from doing. As we grow ourselves up—learning to tolerate uncertainty, step back thoughtfully, and trust children's developing capacities—we create the emotional space in which they can grow themselves up as well.

Perhaps the film's most psychologically important message is also its simplest: Children still need time and space to bring their own worlds to life.

item.title: 5 Reasons I Do Not Offer Free Phone Consultations
item.description:
Online Therapy

5 Reasons I Do Not Offer Free Phone Consultations

Personal Perspective: The internet has changed how consumers approach therapy.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • 15-20 minutes is not sufficient to determine what needs to be determined subconsciously.
  • The medium is the message and therapist platforms have trained patients with new expectations.
  • "Psychological Man" doesn't join or commit to things; he samples them like he's at a Las Vegas buffet.

"The best lack all conviction, while the worst are full of passionate intensity." —W.B. Yeats, "The Second Coming"

In 1986 through 1988, I studied "The Aesthetics of Authority" with Philip Rieff at the University of Pennsylvania. In Professor Rieff's book The Triumph of the Therapeutic, he prophetically posited that "Psychological Man" (that's us) doesn't commit to things — he samples smorgasbords of things as if he's in Las Vegas going buffet to buffet. Psychological Man relates to institutions the way consumers relate to apps — always expecting free trial periods — and to Amazon, always expecting money-back guarantees. Someone asking for a free consultation from a psychotherapist "to see if we're a match" is behaving exactly as the Internet culture has trained them to behave and just as Professor Rieff predicted.

From my point of view as a psychotherapist with 18 years of private practice experience, if a potential patient thinks that their time is too valuable for them to come into my office and sit eyeball to eyeball with me, then I can tell in advance that we're probably not a match.

Here are the 5 reasons why I stopped offering free telephone consultations:

  1. "The eyes are the windows to the soul." UCLA psychologist Albert Mehrabian's well-known 7-38-55 rule found that when people are communicating feelings and attitudes, only 7% of the message comes through the actual words spoken — the remaining 93% comes through tone of voice (38%) and body language and facial expression (55%). A 15-20 minute phone consultation in the best case scenario would only give the potential client 45% - tone plus verbally transmitted data - of the information that they need to make a decision.
  2. 15-20 minutes is not sufficient to determine if someone is "a member of your tribe," which is what the patient is testing for subconsciously. To be able to truly trust a psychotherapist with your darkest secrets and be assured that they will understand and respect your mental and emotional experiences, you first have to subconsciously sense that they speak your language and can empathize with you. Therapists know that rapport and trust-building — especially with patients who have had their trust violated or betrayed early in life — can take up to a year or more. Fifteen to twenty minutes on the phone is not enough time to determine what needs to be determined subconsciously.
  3. The essential service that psychotherapists provide, in my humble opinion, is mirroring and matching: mirroring the patient's facial affect and matching the patient's body language. As I wrote in How To Survive Your Childhood Now That You're An Adult: A Path to Authenticity and Awakening, "Mirror neurons do not fire via text message." We are trained to validate our patients' emotional experiences and get the mirror neurons firing so that the patients know that they're not the only ones who feel this way. The world is a crazy place and in our "normal" interactions with other human beings our emotions are often inadvertently invalidated; on one level, therapy provides a safe space for emotional tune-ups, to have another human being empathize with you. As Krishnamurti famously said, "It is no measure of health to be well-adjusted to a profoundly sick society." Therapists hold and contain your maladjustments.
  4. Nobody truly understands the psychology underneath financial transactions, but Freud had a rule that many of his heirs have forgotten: Freud believed that money was an important part of the therapeutic container, the "frame". Without a real cost, the patient had nothing at stake and a relationship with nothing at stake produces resistance, not progress. If you remove the money then you turn the analyst from a professional into a benefactor and the patient from an agent into a charity case. In "On Beginning the Treatment," Freud argued that an absent fee increases resistance and undermines both the patient's motivation and the therapeutic relationship.
  5. We've all heard of the paradox of choice; do you think you're overwhelmed choosing between Hulu, HBO, AppleTV, Paramount, Disney, Netflix and all of your entertainment options? A free trial period may be a perfectly reasonable expectation to help you decide on a movie app or a dating app but I don't think it's appropriate for a licensed mental healthcare provider.

And speaking of dating apps…if you haven’t noticed, most therapist platforms vaguely resemble Match.com with a grid of headshots and seductive bios. For people who have been trained on Tinder and Hinge to treat profiles as invitations to swipe (mostly reject and avoid), the medium is the message and the interface instructs the behavior.

Obviously being a good "match" with your therapist is incredibly important, but hundreds of my articles, thousands of my videos, hundreds of interviews are available online for free...why is it that someone will summon AI to summarize Reddit reviews and spend twenty minutes hunting down the best new gourmet pizza joint in the neighborhood but can't be bothered to Google a therapist's name?

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Psychiatry Is Not an Exact Science
item.description:
Psychiatry

Why Psychiatry Is Not an Exact Science

Over time, mental illnesses have become understood in increasing detail.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Psychiatry is less exact than sciences like chemistry, with diagnoses and definitions evolving over time.
  • Mental disorders often lack clear causes and may defy classification, as seen with pseudologia fantastica.
  • Pseudologues in power could erode trust and disrupt organizations due to their persistent fantastic lying.

“Isn’t it true, doctor, that medicine is an inexact science?” Anyone testifying in court as an expert witness can expect that question at some point in their cross-examination. The correct answer is “Yes.”

Few, if any, of the specialty areas of medicine achieve the exactitude of chemistry, mathematics, physics, mechanical engineering, or even architecture. A well-constructed bridge will remain in place for perhaps centuries, while a surgical operation may be performed flawlessly, but the patient may nonetheless die due to conditions beyond the surgeon’s control.

An absence of exactitude is especially inherent in diseases of neuropsychiatric origin. This starts with deciding what the disease should be named. Physicians in the 19th century had a predilection for naming diseases after the practitioner who first recognized and described them. Thus, today we have the eponymous Parkinson’s disease named after the surgeon James Parkinson, who in 1817 published “An Essay on the Shaking Palsy.” Decades later, eminent neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot renamed paralysis agitans as Parkinson’s disease in his honor.

Next came descriptions based on part of the brain affected by a specific disease, such as spinocerebellar ataxia (a loss of balance and impairment in walking secondary to the involvement of nerve tracts within the spinal cord and the cerebellum, an organ toward the back of the brain partially responsible for balance).

Currently, diseases are frequently described and named based on the genes found to cause them. Many neuropsychiatric diseases that were formerly viewed as a singular disorder are now understood as a spectrum, in some cases involving many genetic expressions. Autism, once considered a unitary illness, is now viewed as a spectrum disorder involving many genetic contributors and different symptoms. In addition, Alzheimer’s, schizophrenia, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) have been shown to include genetically distinct variants of the diseases.

But on occasion, a condition turns up in neuropsychiatry without any indicator of its origin, certainly no abnormality that the foremost students of neuropsychiatric disease can agree upon. In fact, in some cases, unanimity doesn’t extend even to the belief that the condition results from a brain disturbance. For example, take what’s described as pseudologia fantastica.

In 1891, German psychiatrist Anton Delbrück published a series of cases marked by autobiographical falsehoods that blended truth and near-truth with outlandish and extravagant claims that seem fantastical to anyone hearing them. Further investigations revealed that these untruths are held with absolute certainty. In most cases, the patient gains nothing from the lies and frequently suffers negative consequences when they are revealed. No reason for this lying can be established; typically, the lies involve matters that people would consider not worth lying about, such as how many people attended a gala party, especially when no party took place. Delbrück named the condition pseudologia fantastica, which translates to false speech or discourse involving imaginative or fantastic elements. It’s called, most appropriately, “pathological imaginative lying.”

Most striking is the rarity of pseudologia fantastica. A 1988 review of the disorder marked the first review in over 50 years. That review noted that only 26 reports had been published since Delbrück’s original description. Although various mental disorders have been suggested to be the cause of pseudologia fantastica, the diagnosis eludes classification, one of the reasons the condition has never been included in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM).

Imagine if a pseudologue were in the position of a CEO. After many examples of being caught in lies over weeks, months, or even years, if they aren’t identified early enough, increasingly elaborate lying with each passing day creates an atmosphere of distrust and conflict that can permeate the entire organization. The lies may serve as esteem boosters for the pseudologue.

What makes pseudologia fantastica so important is the effect the pseudologue exerts on others. Eventually, in response to the pseudologue’s lies and exaggerations, people don’t know what to think. As a result, they begin to doubt just about anything they are told. As George Orwell noted in his novel 1984, not believing anything often coexists with a tendency to believe anything. Since pseudologia fantastica is not a common condition and the inveterate lying may occur in people who appear otherwise normal, it may slip beneath the radar of suspicion.

Since pseudologia fantastica is not a recognized DSM mental illness, options for dealing with it are limited: medicine, especially psychiatry, is not an exact science, remember?

Richard M. Restak, M.D.

item.title: How to Navigate the Freshman 15
item.description:
Adolescence

How to Navigate the Freshman 15

It's very common for college freshmen to gain weight.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Freshman year of college involves much group activity, which leads to increased food consumption.
  • In college, disrupted sleep patterns and schedules contribute to poor eating habits.
  • College students returning home for the summer are well aware of the weight gain; do not body shame them.

Adolescents are preparing to go off to college very soon, and the kids and their parents are anxious and excited. I try to provide as much support as possible for the kids and their parents. The idea of leaving home and leaving friends and family is a lot to deal with. The adolescents are worried about making new friends, whether or not they will get along with their roommates, and what it will be like not having their parents and being in unfamiliar surroundings. The structure of their day and who they will go to meals with is also a major concern. The parents share similar concerns and worry about whether or not their kids will adjust well, be safe, and use good judgment.

This brings to mind another issue that parents ask me about all the time. Many of the girls, and the boys as well, come home at the end of the year with an extra 15 pounds. Clearly, this is not an issue for everyone, but it is for many. I remember shopping for jeans at the end of my freshman year. I was stunned that I had gone up three sizes. I remember eating well and running that summer so I was back to my usual weight at the beginning of sophomore year. Last year, I worked with at least two students who were embarrassed about their weight gain and were afraid to go home. In one case, the mother was understanding, as she too had gained weight during her freshman year of college. In the other case, the mother body shamed the child, whose anxiety then escalated. At that point, the mother and daughter came to session together, and the situation settled down.

Parents ask why this happens and how to address this with their kids. This weight change happens for many reasons, but Herman (2017) provides excellent insight. He explains that when people eat in groups, they tend to eat more. And, in college, there is lots of group eating. Additionally, there is an endless amount of food available in college cafeterias. When college kids eat together, they often stay at meals longer in an effort to both socialize and perhaps avoid studying. Part of the college experience also includes ordering food late at night, and this happens with significantly less frequency at home. I remember that we all ate snacks while studying as both an adjunct activity and in an effort to stay awake. College freshmen often get little sleep as they stay up too late socializing and sometimes studying. Additionally, there may be increased alcohol consumption associated with more parties and, hence, weight gain.

Parents often worry about how to respond to this weight change. My major concern is that you not body shame your child. Gaining the freshman 15 is sort of a rite of passage and is certainly preferable to a child coming home anorexic. By sophomore year, your child is much more likely to have developed a structured schedule that includes time carved out for exercise, studying, meals, and hopefully healthy sleeping habits. Your child is well aware of his/her body change. You can certainly model healthy eating habits, but discussion of their weight gain should be avoided. The kids are already painfully aware. Instead, I suggest focusing on discussing the highlights of their freshman year and the struggles that they choose to discuss with you.

item.title: Finding Meaning in Your Own Odyssey
item.description:
Resilience

Finding Meaning in Your Own Odyssey

Life is an odyssey into the unexpected.

Posted July 4, 2026

Key points
  • Life is an adventure to be embraced and experienced to the fullest.
  • Through difficulties, we can discover other sides of ourselves.
  • The return to our core essence is our final destination.
Source: Michelle Maria/Pixabay

Two of the oldest literary works, Iliad and Odyssey, were written in the seventh century B.C. by Homer, a Greek poet. Now, a film adaptation of Homer’s epic tale, The Odyssey, is set to be released in summer 2026. The story focuses on Odysseus, the Greek King of Ithaka, and his 10-year journey home after the Trojan War. Along the way, Odysseus faced many challenges, such as lotus narcotic plants (which caused his shipmates to lose any desire for action), the one-eyed giant Cyclops, Sirens, Calypso, and Circe, who all impeded his return to his homeland, the place where he belonged.

It is Homer whom we must thank for giving us the popular word “odyssey” and its deeper meaning, which is now associated with the idea of traveling along life’s uncharted path. And like Odysseus, I view life as an odyssey into the unexpected, as well as an adventure to be embraced and experienced to the fullest. Importantly, our odysseys help us answer the existential question, “How do I live a more meaningful life?”

Facing Our Challenges

In The Odyssey, Odysseus faced 12 challenges. Many of us have faced at least 12 challenges in our own lives, times when we have been called upon to overcome obstacles and difficulties. Challenges test us; we can either retreat in fear or we can rise up. It is during these times in life when we have to find the courage to move through our fears.

As the philosopher Epictetus taught us, difficulties show us who we are. We can discover other sides of ourselves and gain a deeper sense of faith in ourselves. Many times, after the fact, we come to realize that challenges were placed in front of us so that we could discover something very important and meaningful about ourselves and our world.

When our minds are focused on something greater than ourselves, on a goal that is truly meaningful, we are often able to summon the courage to move forward. There are also many ways we can add deep and meaningful value to the lives of others and, in doing so, add deep value and meaning to our own lives. We have to look for, and be open to, opportunities to serve and to make a positive, meaningful difference in the life of the next person we encounter—a “pay it forward” way of living.

Core Essence

The human quest for meaning can be viewed as a personal odyssey, and much like Odysseus’ return to Ithaka, the return to our core essence is the final destination. In other words, our true nature has always been there, and through our different experiences, it reveals itself slowly and deliberately as we evolve.

We are all born with our unique, core essence, but the choices we make in life can either serve to conceal or reveal this essence. When we wear “masks,” pretending to live someone else’s life or trying to keep up with others, we lose sense of our true selves, and, tragically, we disconnect from that part of ourselves that makes us unique. In turn, this affects, in negative ways, our ability to be comfortable with who we are and to connect meaningfully with others.

When we ask more questions and examine our lives like Socrates encouraged us to do, we begin to gain more clarity about our place in the world and what unique traits and talents we can share with the world. Asking questions helps us to determine if we need to let go of certain beliefs or situations that no longer work for us. As we explore who we are, we can go beyond the limits of who we are allowing ourselves to be and expand into our fuller selves. This helps us live in harmony with ourselves and others and ultimately to live with more meaning.

When we focus on the difficulties of life and on what’s wrong or what’s missing, we lose power and energy. We get stuck, like Odysseus did, in a swirling whirlpool, repeating the same motions and not moving forward. When we procrastinate, waiting for the situation to be “right,” standing on the sidelines of life, we lose valuable time and experiences.

As we begin to understand what is meaningful—what really matters to us—we begin to transform and enter the process of becoming who we are really meant to be. When we understand and act from our own Core of Meaning, we become more engaged and resilient, more energetic and healthy, more creative and productive.

As Homer taught us in the Odyssey, everyone’s journey is unique. With perseverance and courage, we can become more fully ourselves and truly know that our lives are meaningful, to ourselves and to others.
